steps_raw.instruction: For each sample, excise the band from the gel that contains the PCR product. The NET-seq library is a broad band that runs at ~150 nt (use oGAB as baseline and cut up ~50 nt). steps_raw.title: 3.4.10 PCR product cleanup
steps_raw.instruction: Precipitate the NET-seq library by adding 2 µl of 15 mg/ml GlycoBlue and 680 µl of isopropanol. Mix well then incubate the precipitations at −20 °C for ≥1 h (the DNA precipitations can be stored at −20 °C overnight).

steps_raw.title: 3.4.10 PCR product cleanup
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge at 20,000g for 30 min at 4 °C to pellet the RNA.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.10 PCR product cleanup
steps_raw.instruction: Remove the supernatant and wash the pellet with 750 µl of 80% (vol/vol) ice-cold ethanol.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.10 PCR product cleanup
steps_raw.instruction: Spin the sample at 20,000g for 2 min at 4 °C, and then remove the supernatant. Air-dry the RNA pellet for 10 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.10 PCR product cleanup
steps_raw.instruction: Resuspend the NET-seq library in 7 - 10 µl of Tris-HCl (10 mM, pH 8.0). The DNA sequencing library can be stored indefinitely at −20 °C.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.11 Quantification and characterization of NET-seq library (Figure 4)
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare a 1:5 dilution of the NET-seq library by adding 1 µl of the NET-seq library to 4 µl of Tris-HCl (10 mM, pH 8.0); mix well (see Note 40).

steps_raw.title: 3.4.11 Quantification and characterization of NET-seq library (Figure 4)
steps_raw.instruction: Use 1 µl of the diluted NET-seq library for quantification with the Qubit fluorometer using the Qubit dsDNA HS assay kit. Prepare the sample and perform the measurement according to the manufacturer’s protocol (see Note 41).

steps_raw.title: 3.4.11 Quantification and characterization of NET-seq library (Figure 4)
steps_raw.instruction: Use 1 µl of the diluted NET-seq library for characterization on the Agilent Bioanalyzer; use the high-sensitivity DNA analysis kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.11 Quantification and characterization of NET-seq library (Figure 4)
steps_raw.instruction: Sequence using oLSC006. Sequence the human NET-seq library from the 3′ end (single-end sequencing) on the Illumina platform using oLSC006 (Table 1) as a custom sequencing primer. Perform sequencing according to the manufacturer’s instructions. NET-seq libraries are typically sequenced on MiSeq, HiSeq or NextSeq next-generation sequencing platforms. A reasonable coverage is obtained with 100–200 million reads.

steps_raw.title: 3.5 Bioinformatics analysis (Figure 5)
steps_raw.instruction: Below we describe in brief the custom bioinformatics pipeline (see Figure 5) that is used to generate NET-seq coverage files. The scripts are available at http://github.com/churchmanlab/MiMB2019NETseq . See Note 42 for a description of the improvements relative to our previous pipeline (Mayer et al. 2015) .

steps_raw.title: 3.5.1 Alignment of sequencing reads
steps_raw.instruction: Assess read quality control with FastQC.

steps_raw.title: 3.5.1 Alignment of sequencing reads
steps_raw.instruction: Displace 5’ end random barcode sequence from sequence to read identifier line and save as a separate fastq file. This barcode serves as a unique molecular identifier (UMI) and originates from the linker (see Table 1).

steps_raw.title: 3.5.1 Alignment of sequencing reads
steps_raw.instruction: Align fastq files with and without UMI sequences separately to a human reference genome using STAR (See Note 43). In case a Drosophila spike-in was used, concatenate the human and Drosophila fasta files to generate a combined reference genome.

steps_raw.title: 3.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments resulting from RT mispriming events, i.e. cases where RT priming did not occur at the complementary sequence site on the ligated linker but instead at a position within the RNA fragment. The resulting reads can be identified as they lack the random UMI sequence encoded on the linker and therefore align well to the reference genome both with and without UMI displacement: when the STAR alignment score of a read with the UMI sequence equals the UMI length (10nt) plus the alignment score from that read without UMI.

steps_raw.title: 3.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments that map to multiple genomic locations by filtering for their MAPQ value (

steps_raw.title: 3.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments resulting from PCR duplication events, i.e. cases of multiple amplicons that originate from the same RNA fragment. The resulting multiple reads are bioinformatically indistinguishable as their alignments share the same position, strand, chromosome, UMI sequence and CIGAR score. To filter out these PCR duplicates, we maintain only one of the alignments.

steps_raw.title: 3.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments that could arise from splicing intermediates, i.e. 3’ ends of annotated exons and introns.

steps_raw.title: 3.5.3 Determine RNA polymerase coverage genome-wide from read alignments.
steps_raw.instruction: Use HTseq to generate a coverage (bedgraph) file containing the read counts at a base-pair resolution over the reference genome as determined from the 5’ end of the read alignments (without UMI) on the opposite strand. The resulting positions correspond to the 3’ ends of nascent RNA and thereby map RNA polymerase positions. The coverage files will be used for a variety of downstream bioinformatics analyses such as visual inspection (e.g. using IGV), metagene profiling (e.g. Bedtools), differential expression (e.g. DEseq2).

steps_raw.title: Box 1 | Western blot control: checking cell fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: The western blot control is used to determine whether or not the cellular fractionation protocol has been executed successfully. The efficiency of the fractionation can be quantified by measuring the amount of elongating Pol II captured in the chromatin fraction (ideally≥95%). When the fractionation protocol is being performed for the first time or being tested on a new cell type, the cytoplasm, nucleoplasm, and chromatin fractions should be checked for subcellular marker proteins (see Note 5) to confirm the fractionation is working (see Note 20).

steps_raw.title: Box 1 | Western blot control: checking cell fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: Adjust the nucleoplasmic (from 3.3.2) and chromatin fraction (from 3.3.2) volumes to the cytoplasmic fraction (from 3.3.1) volume by adding 1× PBS. Mix each fraction well and ensure the chromatin pellet is completely resuspended (see Note 7).

steps_raw.title: Box 1 | Western blot control: checking cell fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: Add 50 µl of 2× SDS buffer (see section 2.3.2 step 7) to 50 µl of each subcellular fraction and boil the samples at 95 °C for 5 min (at this point, samples can be stored for months at −20 °C).

steps_raw.title: Box 1 | Western blot control: checking cell fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: Separate samples by standard SDS-PAGE (loading 10 µl of each boiled sample per lane is usually sufficient).

steps_raw.title: Box 1 | Western blot control: checking cell fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: Probe the membrane overnight at 4 °C with Pol II CTD Ser2-P antibody (3E10, 1:1,000 dilution) and Pol II CTD Ser5-P antibody (3E8, 1:1,000 dilution). These antibodies target transcribing RNA Pol II (see Note 6).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Performing RNA fragmentation results in a homogeneous RNA pool which helps to avoid length biases in any downstream enzymatic reactions. The fragmentation test can be performed using total RNA (or any easily-obtained RNA sample). Once the appropriate fragmentation time is determined (where most of the RNA molecules range from 40 –110 nt), fragmentation can be performed on the nascent RNA (obtained from cellular fractionation) using the determined time (Figure 2); the size range of the nascent RNA and total RNA pools do not vary enough for the fragmentation time to be different.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Take 9 samples of RNA from a total RNA sample (or any other easily obtained RNA sample), each sample should be 20 µl in volume and contain ~1ug of RNA. Add 20 µl of 2× alkaline fragmentation solution to each sample and mix well (see Note 32); fragmentation is not performed for the oGAB11 control.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Fragment each RNA sample at 95 °C in a thermal cycler for the following times: 0, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, and 50 minutes.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: To purify the fragmented RNA, use the RNA Clean & Concentrator-5 kit (Zymo) and elute RNA from column with 10 uL of 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.0). Alternatively, RNA can be prepared by RNA precipitation (see Note 33).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare RNA ladder (denoted as L in figure) by adding 1.0 µl of RNA control ladder to 9 µl of RNase-free H2O. Add 10 µl of 2× TBU denaturing sample to the RNA ladder and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare all RNA samples by adding 1.0 µl of 2× TBU denaturing sample buffer to each sample, mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Denature the RNA sample and RNA ladder for 2 min at 80 °C. Place the samples on ice.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Pre-run a 15% (wt/vol) polyacrylamide TBE-urea gel at 200 V for 15 min in 1× TBE. Thoroughly flush out gel wells prior to pre-running the gel (see Note 35).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Load gel with the RNA ladder and the fragmented RNA sample. Separate by PAGE at 200 V for 65 min.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Stain the gel in 50 ml of gel staining solution for 5 min at room temperature on a shaker (use a black gel box to protect gel from light while staining).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Visualize the gel under blue/UV light. The optimal fragmentation time is when most RNA molecules are in the required size range, between 40 and 110 nt (the optimal fragmentation time in the figure below is between 25 and 30 minutes).

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: This protocol for rapidly extracting RNA or cDNA from a polyacrylamide TBE-urea gel is similar to the gel extraction protocol described by the Weissman laboratory (Ingolia et al. 2012; Churchman and Weissman 2012) .

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Use a 21G needle to pierce the bottom of a 0.5-ml RNase-free microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Place the pierced 0.5-ml tube into a 1.5-ml RNase-free microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Put the gel slice (from fragmentation, RT, or PCR) into the pierced 0.5-ml tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge the nestled tubes, containing the gel slice, at 20,000g for 4 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Add 200 µl of RNase-free H2O to the chopped-up gel and mix.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Incubate the sample mixture for 10 min at 70 °C in a Thermomixer.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Vortex the mixture for 30 s at medium intensity.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Cut the tip off of a 1,000-µl pipette tip and transfer the gel mixture into a microcentrifuge tube filter.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge the mixture at 20,000g for 3 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: The NET-seq library is PCR amplified using an Illumina index forward primer (Barcode primer, see Table 1) and a reverse primer (oNTI231; Table 1) specific to NET-seq (Figure 4). For each NET-seq library preparation, the minimum number of PCR cycles needed to obtain a sequencing library must to be determined. The NET-seq library is then amplified with the determined minimal amount of PCR cycles; this avoids overamplification which can result in unwanted products such as PCR duplicates.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare the PCR master mix (see section 2.4.8 step 4) for four pilot PCR amplifications for each cDNA sample and the oGAB11 cDNA control sample (denoted as O in figure). Mix well and store it on ice.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: For each PCR sample, put 19 µl of PCR master mix in a 0.2-ml RNase-free PCR tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Add 1 µl of circularized cDNA and mix it well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Perform PCR pilot amplifications (described in Table 2). Remove one PCR tube for each sample at the end of the extension step after 6, 8, 10 and 12 amplification cycles.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Add 3.4 µl of 6× DNA loading dye to each tube and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare DNA control ladder (denoted as L in figure) by adding 1.0 µl of ladder to 9 µl of DNase-free H2O. Then add 2 µl of 6× DNA loading dye and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Separate the PCR products and the DNA control ladder by TBE gel electrophoresis on an 8% (wt/vol) TBE gel at 180 V for 55 min.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Stain the gel in 50 ml of gel staining solution (see section 2.4.8) for 5 min at room temperature on a shaker (use a black gel box to protect gel from light while staining).

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Visualize the gel under blue/UV light and identify the optimal PCR amplification cycles for each cDNA sequencing library. The optimal PCR amplification cycles for the NET-seq library, which runs at ~150 nt, is determined by the presence of a clear band at ~150 nt and no higher-molecular-weight PCR products (the optimal number of cycles in the figure below is between 6 and 8).

steps_raw.title: 1.2 Preparation of cells for fractionation
steps_raw.instruction: Cellular fractionation has been successfully performed on several different cell types (see Note 19 in the Guidelines section). The protocol was originally optimized for HeLa S3 or HEK293T cells (Mayer and Churchman 2016) . When fractionating other cell types optimization may be required (see Note 20). Cells are ideally grown according to internationally recognized guidelines (such as those suggested by ENCODE) and handled according to the supplier’s instructions (see Note 21 in the Guidelines section).

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: The following steps are for suspension cells, if working with adherent cells see Note 22 for steps on how to prepare the cells.

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Count out 1×107 cells as input for each fractionation, including a western blot control sample (see Note 23). If cell numbers are limited, fractionation can be performed on fewer cells (see Note 24).

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Collect cells by centrifugation at 500g for 2 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Wash with 10 ml of PBS (room temperature).

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Collect cells by centrifugation at 500g for 2 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Add spike-in cells (Drosophila S2, used for normalization) to the sample cells collected by centrifugation (the addition of a spike-in is optional, see Note 25).

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Repeat wash (step 3) and centrifugation (step 4).

steps_raw.title: 3.2.1 Washing and counting cells
steps_raw.instruction: Remove supernatant by aspiration. It is important to remove the supernatant completely to avoid diluting the lysis buffer (see Note 26).
3.3 Cellular Fractionation (Figure 1a)

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Using a cut P1000 pipette tip, add 200 µl of CLB to cells and mix by pipetting the sample up and down ten times. Transfer sample to an RNase-free 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube using a cut 1,000 µl pipette tip.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Incubate the cell lysate on ice for 5 min.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: During incubation period, pipette 500 µl of SB to an RNase-free 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: After incubation period, use a cut 1,000 µl pipette tip to layer the cell lysate sample onto the SB (see Note 27).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge layered lysate at 16,000g for 10 min at 4 °C to collect nuclei.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Pipette off supernatant completely from the nuclei pellet (supernatant contains the cytoplasmic fraction, retain for western blot, described in Box 1)

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Wash nuclei pellet with 800 µl of NWB (either by inverting the tube or pipetting up and down).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Collect cell nuclei by centrifugation at 1,150g for 1 min at 4 °C.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.1 Isolation of nuclei fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Pipette off supernatant from the nuclei pellet. It is important to remove the supernatant completely in order to remove cytoplasmic mature RNAs (see Note 26).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Add 200 µl of GB to the nuclei. Use a cut 1,000 µl tip to resuspend the washed nuclei pellet by pipetting up and down.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Transfer the nuclei suspension to a new 1.5 ml RNase-free microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Layer 200 µl of NLB onto nuclei suspension and mix by pulsed vortexing.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Incubate the mixture on ice for 2 min.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge at 18,500g for 2 min at 4 °C to collect the chromatin pellet.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Pipette off supernatant from the chromatin pellet. It is important to completely remove the supernatant in order to remove nucleoplasmic RNAs (retain supernatant for the nucleoplasm fraction of western blot, described in Box 1).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.2 Isolation of chromatin fraction
steps_raw.instruction: Add 50 µl CRS to the chromatin pellet, transfer pellet in CRS to a new 1.5 ml tube and then resuspend pellet in CRS (see Note 28). Perform this step on the experimental sample (for the preparation of nascent RNA, section 3.3.3) and the control sample (for the western blot analysis, as described in Box 1).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.3 Preparation of nascent RNA
steps_raw.instruction: Add 700 µl of QIAzol (lysis reagent in miRNeasy mini kit, Qiagen) to the resuspended chromatin (see Note 10 re QIAzol).

steps_raw.title: 3.3.3 Preparation of nascent RNA
steps_raw.instruction: Solubilize chromatin pellet by slowly pipetting up and down using a 1-ml syringe with a 22G needle (see Note 29). Mix very carefully (to avoid spilling the sample) until the solution is homogeneous.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.3 Preparation of nascent RNA
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare RNA using the miRNeasy mini kit (or miRNeasy micro kit for small cell numbers, see section 2.3.3 step 2) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, including optional DNase treatment.

steps_raw.title: 3.3.3 Preparation of nascent RNA
steps_raw.instruction: Measure the prepared RNA quantity and quality using a NanoDrop (see Note 30). The RNA yield is usually in the range of 20–30 µg (this can vary quite a lot depending on the type of cells used). If fractionation was performed on less than 1×107 cells (or RNA yield is less than 20 µg) see Note 24 re RNA amount needed to construct sequencing library. Store the isolated RNA at −80 °C (can be stored for months) until ready to construct sequencing library.

steps_raw.title: 3.4 Constructing DNA sequencing library from isolated nascent RNA (Figure 1b)
steps_raw.instruction: Spray down all work surfaces, pipettes, etc. with RNase away

steps_raw.title: 3.4.1 Linker ligation (Figure 2)
steps_raw.instruction: Denature the RNA sample (from the cellular fractionation, section 3.3.3) and 5 µl of the oGAB11 control (10 µM; Table 1) for 2 min at 80 °C in a Thermomixer. Place on ice.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.1 Linker ligation (Figure 2)
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare linker ligation mix for each RNA sample and for oGAB11 in 0.2-ml RNase-free PCR tubes. Mix until reaction is homogeneous, poor mixing will negatively affect the ligation efficiency.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.1 Linker ligation (Figure 2)
steps_raw.instruction: Add 1 µl Truncated T4 RNA ligase 2 (200U) to each RNA sample as well as the oGAB11 control.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.1 Linker ligation (Figure 2)
steps_raw.instruction: Incubate the ligation mixes for 10 - 16 hours at 16 °C in a thermal cycler (Note 31).

steps_raw.title: 3.4.1 Linker ligation (Figure 2)
steps_raw.instruction: Place on ice and add 0.7 µl of EDTA (0.5 M) to each ligation mix to stop the ligation reaction.

steps_raw.title: 3.4.2 RNA fragmentation (Figure 2)

steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments resulting from RT mispriming events, i.e. cases where RT priming did not occur at the complementary sequence site on the ligated linker but instead at a position within the RNA fragment. The resulting reads can be identified as they lack the random UMI sequence encoded on the linker and therefore align well to the reference genome both with and without UMI displacement: when the STAR alignment score of a read with the UMI sequence equals the UMI length (10nt) plus the alignment score from that read without UMI.

steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments that map to multiple genomic locations by filtering for their MAPQ value (

steps_raw.title: 1.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments resulting from PCR duplication events, i.e. cases of multiple amplicons that originate from the same RNA fragment. The resulting multiple reads are bioinformatically indistinguishable as their alignments share the same position, strand, chromosome, UMI sequence and CIGAR score. To filter out these PCR duplicates, we maintain only one of the alignments.

steps_raw.title: 1.5.2 Filter out read alignments that do not reflect RNA polymerase position.
steps_raw.instruction: Remove alignments that could arise from splicing intermediates, i.e. 3’ ends of annotated exons and introns.

steps_raw.title: 1.5.3 Determine RNA polymerase coverage genome-wide from read alignments.
steps_raw.instruction: Use HTseq to generate a coverage (bedgraph) file containing the read counts at a base-pair resolution over the reference genome as determined from the 5’ end of the read alignments (without UMI) on the opposite strand. The resulting positions correspond to the 3’ ends of nascent RNA and thereby map RNA polymerase positions. The coverage files will be used for a variety of downstream bioinformatics analyses such as visual inspection (e.g. using IGV), metagene profiling (e.g. Bedtools), differential expression (e.g. DEseq2).

steps_raw.instruction: Take 9 samples of RNA (~1ug each) from a total RNA sample (or any other easily obtained RNA sample). Re-suspend each RNA sample in 8uL of RNase-free water and add 12uL of the linker ligation mix, excluding the linker and ligase (see Materials section 1.4.1, Linker ligation, step 4). Add 20 µl of 2× alkaline fragmentation solution (see Materials section 1.4.2 , RNA fragmentation, step 1) to each sample and mix well (see Note 32 in the Guidelines section); fragmentation is not performed for the oGAB11 control.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Fragment each RNA sample at 95 °C in a thermal cycler for the following times: 0, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, and 50 minutes.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: To purify the fragmented RNA, use the RNA Clean & Concentrator-5 kit (Zymo) and elute RNA from column with 10 uL of 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.0). Alternatively, RNA can be prepared by RNA precipitation (see Note 33 in the Guidelines section).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare RNA ladder (denoted as L in figure) by adding 1.0 µl of RNA control ladder to 9 µl of RNase-free H2O. Add 10 µl of 2× TBU denaturing sample to the RNA ladder and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare all RNA samples by adding 10 µl of 2× TBU denaturing sample buffer to each sample, mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Denature the RNA sample and RNA ladder for 2 min at 80 °C. Place the samples on ice.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Pre-run a 15% (wt/vol) polyacrylamide TBE-urea gel at 200 V for 15 min in 1× TBE. Thoroughly flush out gel wells prior to pre-running the gel (see Note 35 in the Guidelines section).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Load gel with the RNA ladder and the fragmented RNA sample. Separate by PAGE at 200 V for 65 min.

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Stain the gel in 50 ml of gel staining solution for 5 min at room temperature on a shaker (use a black gel box to protect gel from light while staining).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Visualize the gel under blue/UV light. The optimal fragmentation time is when most RNA molecules are in the required size range, between 40 and 110 nt (the optimal fragmentation time in the figure below is between 25 and 30 minutes).

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Use a 21G needle to pierce the bottom of a 0.5-ml RNase-free microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Place the pierced 0.5-ml tube into a 1.5-ml RNase-free microcentrifuge tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Put the gel slice (from fragmentation, RT, or PCR) into the pierced 0.5-ml tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge the nestled tubes, containing the gel slice, at 20,000g for 4 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Add 200 µl of RNase-free H2O to the chopped-up gel and mix.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Incubate the sample mixture for 10 min at 70 °C in a Thermomixer.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Vortex the mixture for 30 s at medium intensity.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Cut the tip off of a 1,000-µl pipette tip and transfer the gel mixture into a microcentrifuge tube filter.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: Centrifuge the mixture at 20,000g for 3 min at room temperature.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare the PCR master mix (see Materials section 1.4.8, PCR amplification, step 4) for four pilot PCR amplifications for each cDNA sample and the oGAB11 cDNA control sample (denoted as O in figure). Mix well and store it on ice.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: For each PCR sample, put 19 µl of PCR master mix in a 0.2-ml RNase-free PCR tube.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Add 1 µl of circularized cDNA and mix it well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Perform PCR pilot amplifications (described in Table 2). Remove one PCR tube for each sample at the end of the extension step after 6, 8, 10 and 12 amplification cycles.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Add 3.4 µl of 6× DNA loading dye to each tube and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Prepare DNA control ladder (denoted as L in figure) by adding 1.0 µl of ladder to 9 µl of DNase-free H2O. Then add 2 µl of 6× DNA loading dye and mix well.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Separate the PCR products and the DNA control ladder by TBE gel electrophoresis on an 8% (wt/vol) TBE gel at 180 V for 55 min.

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Stain the gel in 50 ml of gel staining solution (see Materials section 1.4.8, PCR amplification) for 5 min at room temperature on a shaker (use a black gel box to protect gel from light while staining).

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: Visualize the gel under blue/UV light and identify the optimal PCR amplification cycles for each cDNA sequencing library. The optimal PCR amplification cycles for the NET-seq library, which runs at ~150 nt, is determined by the presence of a clear band at ~150 nt and no higher-molecular-weight PCR products (the optimal number of cycles in the figure above is between 6 and 8).

steps_raw.title: 1.5 Bioinformatics analysis (Figure 5)
steps_raw.instruction: Below we describe in brief the custom bioinformatics pipeline (see Figure 5) that is used to generate NET-seq coverage files. The scripts are available at Churchman lab GitHub . See Note 42 in the Guidelines section for a description of the improvements relative to our previous pipeline (Mayer et al. 2015).

steps_raw.title: Box 2 | Fragmentation test
steps_raw.instruction: Performing RNA fragmentation results in a homogeneous RNA pool which helps to avoid length biases in any downstream enzymatic reactions. The fragmentation test can be performed using total RNA (or any easily-obtained RNA sample). Once the appropriate fragmentation time is determined (where most of the RNA molecules range from 40 –110 nt), fragmentation can be performed on the nascent RNA (obtained from cellular fractionation) using the determined time (see directly above); the size range of the nascent RNA and total RNA pools do not vary enough for the fragmentation time to be different.

steps_raw.title: Box 3 | Rapid gel extraction
steps_raw.instruction: This protocol for rapidly extracting RNA or cDNA from a polyacrylamide TBE-urea gel is similar to the gel extraction protocol described by the Weissman laboratory (Ingolia et al. 2012; Churchman and Weissman 2012).

steps_raw.title: Box 4 | PCR amplification test
steps_raw.instruction: The NET-seq library is PCR amplified using an Illumina index forward primer (Barcode primer, see Table 1 in the Materials section) and a reverse primer (oNTI231; Table 1 in the Materials section) specific to NET-seq (Figure 4). For each NET-seq library preparation, the minimum number of PCR cycles needed to obtain a sequencing library must to be determined. The NET-seq library is then amplified with the determined minimal amount of PCR cycles; this avoids overamplification which can result in unwanted products such as PCR duplicates.
